newsitem.title: GERMANY: German forwarders fear higher insurance liability.
newsitem.headline: German forwarders fear higher insurance liability.

text.p: German freight forwarders face potential financial collapse from a planned 250 percent rise in insurance liability, the country's forwarding association BSL warned on Wednesday.
A proposed increase in maximum liability to 17.90 marks per kg from the current 5 marks will cost forwarders 500 million marks a year in higher insurance premiums, it forecast.
But forwarders would not be able to recover these additional costs from shippers through higher rates due to a massive price war, BSL lawyer Hubert Valder told Reuters in a telephone interview.
The BSL would present its case for revision of the proposed transport law reform, due to come into force in July 1998, to the German justice ministry at a meeting tomorrow Thursday, he said.
The association backed the government's plan to simplify existing transport law but this draft amounted to a re-regulation of a de-regulated market, he added.
"We want to get away from these fixed liability limits," Valder said.
Forwarders with warehouses faced a much higher risk of potential loss than pure transport companies but both would have the same classification under the reform draft, he said.
"The problem with the reforms are the economic consequences. In theory there should be higher prices but reality is different. There is a massive price war and over-capacity on the market," he added.
Since forwarders could not pass on the higher costs to shippers and were barely operating at a profit, any major loss could produce serious financial problems, he noted.
All forwarding activities, including road and rail transport as well as multi-modal transport of air cargo to airports would be affected by the new law, Valder said.
Airlines operating road feeder services within Germany which now had an insurance liability of 80 marks per kg would also face new insurance rules but could see a drop in premiums, he added.
"For forwarders, it will definitely be more expensive but not necessarily for the airlines," he added.
The German justice ministry planned to present a transport law bill to Parliament next spring to come into force in mid-1998, Valder noted.
From July 1, 1998, foreign companies will be permitted to freely operate domestic German transport services under the end of the so-called cabotage ban.
